title: Why an 18-cent coin would beat the dime
description:
Score a set of coins by the fewest coins it takes to make every amount of change from 0 to 99 cents. Pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters average 4.7 coins (99 cents alone takes 9). Swap the dime for an 18-cent coin and the average drops to 3.89, about 17% less change: 36 cents becomes two 18s instead of a quarter, a dime and a penny. The catch: paying biggest coin first stops working on 37 of the 100 amounts, so you have to count properly. Jeffrey Shallit worked this out in 2003 ("What This Country Needs Is an 18c Piece").

Numbers checked in code (fewest coins for every amount by dynamic programming, the greedy failures counted, and 200,000 random amounts simulated). Source: futilitycloset.com/2018/11/20/a-call-for-change/ (summarising Shallit, Mathematical Intelligencer 25(2), 2003)

beats.say: Swap the dime for an 18 cent coin, and carry less change.
Not a rounder number. Not a bigger coin. 18 just fills the gaps.
Here's how you score coins. Take every amount from 0 to 99 cents, and find the fewest coins for each.
With pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, 99 cents takes 9 coins. Across all 100 amounts, you average 4.7.
Now swap the dime for an 18. 36 cents was a quarter, a dime and a penny. Now it's just two 18s.
But there's a catch. Pay the biggest coin first, and 36 turns into a quarter, two nickels and a penny.
That habit fails on 37 amounts out of 100. So you count the smart way.
Do that, and you average 3.89 coins. 17% less change, from one odd coin.
So what's the fewest coins for 72 cents?
